summary:
North Chungcheong Province stands under the national framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: article 92-6 of the Military Criminal Act criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and enforcement has been targeted. In 2017 the military charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The province is where South Korea's sharpest documented trans harm occurred. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, the country's first openly transgender soldier, was found dead at her home in Cheongju on 3 March 2021, aged 23, after being compulsorily discharged in early 2020 when a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. Her challenge to the discharge had been rejected in July 2020. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty. Her death triggered national debate on the treatment of transgender troops.

The official response to her death produced pressure for protection but no change in North Chungcheong's own law. The National Human Rights Commission of Korea honoured her, and prosecutors and activists called for an anti-discrimination bill, then at its eighth attempted introduction since 2007; the June 2020 draft contained gender-identity provisions. South Korea still has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTI organisations can register, but an NGO had to litigate for that right at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Legal gender recognition is available nationally and the surgical condition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are unmarried, overturning an 11-year-old precedent; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling extending healthcare rights to same-sex partners is the main advance in that area.

Restroom access is a live problem in both judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal, that police advice telling a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented anti-LGBT violence concentrates at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors while accusing police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates; 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes a relatively positive overall record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
North Chungcheong's trans-specific profile rests on a single dated incident: the death of Byun Hui-su in Cheongju on 3 March 2021. The province has no separate documented pattern of trans-directed violence, police response or facilities dispute beyond that event, so the case should not be read as evidence of a locally distinctive climate of hostility.

The turbulence the incident produced was national rather than provincial. Public grief and demands for LGBT protections surged after 3 March 2021, and the resulting pressure on the anti-discrimination bill, then at its eighth introduction attempt since 2007, played out in the National Assembly, not in the North Chungcheong Provincial Council. No new provincial law followed the incident.

Comparable evidence from elsewhere in South Korea gives context: Pride-related violence in Incheon and Busan, restroom litigation decided in Seoul, and school-environment research presented in Seoul all illustrate conditions that a visitor to North Chungcheong would encounter under the same national statutes and institutions.
localsOnly:
Residents of North Chungcheong seek legal gender recognition through the national courts, where the 8 May 2024 ruling against a surgery mandate and the 24 November 2022 Supreme Court en banc decision on trans parents now govern. The 2011 requirements that a petitioner be over 20, single and childless no longer hold uniformly.

Same-sex couples resident in the province cannot marry or enter a civil union and cannot jointly adopt children, though the 2024 Constitutional Court decision on same-sex partners' healthcare rights applies nationally.

Transgender residents are barred from military service and, if they serve, are exposed to article 92-6 charges carrying up to two years' imprisonment. The National Human Rights Commission of Korea accepts complaints, and its November 2023 finding on hospitalisation blind spots documents the refusal of the Ministry of Health and Welfare to issue guidelines for transgender patients.

The school-restroom findings presented by DDing Dong on 20 March 2024 describe conditions in South Korean schools generally, including boys' schools, where a 16-year-old trans girl reported holding urine and leaving early. The 2014 and 2018 survey figures on classmate harassment, conversion-therapy referral and year-on-year discrimination apply to LGBTQ youth and transgender adults nationwide.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents North Chungcheong-specific enforcement of article 92-6, provincial police handling of anti-LGBT complaints, or any Pride event held within the province; those points remain unresolved rather than negative findings.

Whether the anti-discrimination bill called for after Byun Hui-su's death has since been introduced or passed is not sourced here; the inventory fixes it at its eighth attempted introduction since 2007 with a June 2020 draft containing gender-identity provisions.

The inventory does not state whether North Chungcheong Province or Cheongju has adopted any local ordinance on anti-discrimination, restrooms or partner recognition, nor does it record the outcome of the government's appeal against the March 2017 NGO registration judgment.

The date of Byun Hui-su's discharge is given as early 2020 with her challenge rejected in July 2020, and the BBC report of 3 March 2021 notes a counsellor raising the alarm after 28 February; the exact sequence of those late-February and 3 March events is not fully resolved in the sources.
